Issues.Body:

Add AddEventListenerAsync with typed event keys to Components.Platform

## Description

This PR implements the Events API Proposal Issue (#69922). It adds `AddEventListenerAsync` to `Window` and `CookieStore`, with the first two events, `Window.StorageEvent` and `CookieStore.ChangeEvent`. The public API is the one in the proposal, and I followed Ilona's answers to its open questions. This text explains the implementation.

### How a listener gets from the browser to .NET

- **One JS module.** `js/Platform.ts` exports `createCallback(callbackReference, shapesJson)`. It is bundled by rollup and shipped as a static web asset, so the project is now `Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Razor`. The module has no family-specific code, and it is 397 bytes after Brotli. `Window` imports it once per scope, when the first listener is added.
- **Shapes.** An event object cannot cross to .NET as it is. Each event key carries a JSON shape that names the properties to copy. Plain objects, arrays, and primitives are copied. Any other object becomes a marker, `{"__unsupported":"<type name>"}`, because a reference created in JS would have no owner to dispose it.
- **Event keys.** `EventType<TTarget, TEvent>` holds the event name and how to add a listener. The key is created by an internal helper that knows the event object type, so the public `AddEventListenerAsync` methods need no trimming annotations. A key of one target does not compile on another.
- **Registrations.** Each call creates an `EventListener<TEvent>`. It owns the JS function and the `DotNetObjectReference`, and it is the `IAsyncDisposable` that the caller gets. Disposing it, or canceling its token, removes the listener. After that, no new call to the listener starts, even if a call was already on its way in Interactive Server.
- **Scope end.** `EventListenerCollection` tracks the live registrations, so disposing the scope removes the ones the app did not. `Window` and `CookieStore` each have one. `Window` creates the collection and the module loader when the first listener is added, so an app that adds no listener pays nothing.
- **Errors.** An exception from a listener is logged at Error level through `ILoggerFactory`, and the listener stays added. `BrowserPlatform` takes an optional `ILoggerFactory` and falls back to `NullLoggerFactory`.

### Things worth a look

- **Cancellation.** The token overload removes the listener when the token is canceled. The removal is posted to the captured `SynchronizationContext` by hand. `useSynchronizationContext: true` is not used, because its `Send` blocks forever when `Cancel` runs on Blazor's renderer context. A test hung on this.
- **Renderer context.** Adding a listener changes unlocked state, so the awaits in `AddEventListenerAsync` keep the renderer's synchronization context. A unit test checks that for `Window` and `CookieStore`.
- **Package changes.** The root `package.json` and `package-lock.json` get one workspace line each for `src/Components/Platform/src/js`, like the other JS projects. `Microsoft.Extensions.Logging.Abstractions` comes from the existing references.
- **Cost on Interactive Server.** Each event is one call from JS to .NET, which is a network message. That is fine for these two events, because they are rare.
- **Not in this PR.** There is no `ForEachAsync` helper, as discussed on the proposal. `FeatureContext` (#69993) is not used yet. When it merges, I will merge `main` and move the event parts into it.

### Tests

- Unit tests (78 in the Platform test project in total) cover the callback bridge, the listener lifecycle (add, remove, cancel before, during, and after the addition, scope end, a failing removal), logging of listener exceptions, and the public API rules.
- Jest tests (8) cover `Platform.ts`.
- E2E tests watch `storage` events fired by another page, and `change` events of the cookie store, in Interactive Server and WebAssembly.
- I ran the unit and E2E tests locally, from the build output and from the output of `dotnet publish`. I also published the WebAssembly test app with trimming and checked that the assembly is trimmed.

Issues.Title: [Review agent] Check cross-render-mode event-ordering differences when synchronous WebAssembly handlers call NavigationManager.NavigateTo on links
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues.

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.

#### Summary

During review of #70299 (`src/Components/Web.JS/src/Services/NavigationEnhancement.ts:104-105`, moving enhanced navigation's `onDocumentClick` listener after `EventDelegator`'s click listener), only one reviewer caught that `<a href="/other" @onclick='() => Nav.NavigateTo("/counter")'>` (without `@onclick:preventDefault`) changes behavior in Interactive WebAssembly (where `@onclick` runs synchronously during the click event and starts programmatic enhanced navigation to `/counter`, which is then aborted when `onDocumentClick` runs second on the un-prevented `<a href="/other">`) while Interactive Server still lands on `/counter` (because `@onclick` runs asynchronously over SignalR after `onDocumentClick`).

#### Root cause

`docs/BlazorComponentsGuidance.md` checks render-mode parity (`Server`, `WebAssembly`, `Auto`, static SSR) and event/navigation ordering separately, but does not call out the interaction between synchronous WebAssembly DOM event dispatch (`invokeMethodAsync` during click) vs. asynchronous Server event dispatch when a DOM listener is reordered relative to `EventDelegator`.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Update `docs/BlazorComponentsGuidance.md` (and evaluate in `eng/skill-evals/review-pull-request/`) so changes to `EventDelegator` / `NavigationEnhancement` listener ordering explicitly check synchronous WebAssembly vs. asynchronous Server handler interaction with default anchor activation.

### Additional context

Issues.Title: [Review agent] Require exact test-endpoint reachability and non-copied fixture delta before keeping test-asset findings
Issues.Body:
### Summary

During Round 2 review of #69721, a reviewer reported and `review-candidate-verifier` returned `KEEP` on a `string.IsNullOrEmpty(lastCode) && code != lastCode` check at `src/Components/test/testassets/Components.TestServer/RemoteMsalAuthenticationStartup.cs:77` (`/subdir/oidc/token`).

### Root Cause

1. **Unreached endpoint in the executed test:** While `RemoteMsalAuthenticationTest` hosts `TrimmingServerFixture<RemoteMsalAuthenticationStartup>`, the active MSAL E2E test only verifies that `AuthenticationService.signIn` is invoked (`__msalSignInCalled`) and stops before completing the authorization-code exchange against `/subdir/oidc/token`. The `/subdir/oidc/token` branch therefore has no effect on any executed test outcome.
2. **Verbatim copy of pre-existing fixture code (`oldVsNew`):** `RemoteMsalAuthenticationStartup.cs:77` is a verbatim copy of existing fixture code in `src/Components/test/testassets/Components.TestServer/RemoteAuthenticationStartup.cs:82` on `main`, which `review-candidate-verifier` treated as `oldVsNew: "n/a"` because it appeared in a newly added startup file.

### Proposed Fix

- For findings in `testassets/**` and `test/**`, require `trigger` and `effect` to prove that an executed test actually reaches the exact route, callback, or branch and that the flaw can affect an observable test outcome (false pass, false failure, flakiness, or masking a product bug under test).
- When a new test fixture copies helper/endpoint code verbatim from an existing fixture in the repository, require `oldVsNew` to account for the existing fixture baseline rather than treating the copied helper as a brand-new defect.

Tracked under #70231.

Issues.Title: [Review agent] Pass PR description and linked issue context to review-candidate-verifier to avoid false intent-downgrade questions
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues.

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe the problem.

#### Summary

During review of #70304 (`Renderer.Dispose` / `DisposeAsync` early return in `Renderer.HandleComponentException` when `_rendererIsDisposed` is set, fixing #66322), `review-candidate-verifier` returned `DOWNGRADE` (`downgradeKind: "intent"`, `confidence: question`) asking whether ignoring `ComponentBase.DispatchExceptionAsync` during synchronous renderer disposal was intended.

#### Root cause

Although `prepare-review.cs` fetches `pull.json` (which links #66322 and states that late `DispatchExceptionAsync` calls during/after renderer disposal should be safely ignored) and the PR includes unit test `DispatchExceptionAsync_DuringRendererDisposal_DoesNotThrow`, the coordinator only passed candidate claims, diff paths, and `docs/*Guidance.md` paths to `review-candidate-verifier`. Under `review-candidate-verifier.agent.md`'s rule that a PR-added test alone establishes PR intent rather than a binding contract, any deliberate bug fix that changes edge-case behavior without an existing `baseTip` doc explicitly requiring the new behavior is downgraded to `intent` (`question`) when the verifier lacks the linked issue / PR intent context.

### Describe the solution you'd like

Include `pull.json` (and linked issue summary when available in the frozen bundle) in the verifier input contract and distinguish addressing the linked bug report's target scenario from unmentioned collateral behavior changes.

### Additional context

Tracked under #70231.

Issues.Title: SignalR stateful reconnect: keep-alive ping can keep holding `HubConnectionContext._writeLock` after reconnect/disconnect
Issues.Body:
With stateful reconnect, a keep-alive ping can be blocked on a full transport pipe when the client reconnects onto a new pipe. The ping is never completed or cancelled. It keeps `_writeLock` held, and the connection can't be torn down, even after the client disconnects.

**Repro**
1. Set `AllowStatefulReconnect=true` on a hub. Connect two clients A and B.
2. Abruptly disconnect A
3. Before the next keep-alive ping, from B, send enough bytes to leave the connection just under the `PauseWriterThreshold`, such that the next keep-alive ping should take it over the threshold.
   - The default `PauseWriterThreshold` is 65536 bytes - writing 65530 bytes should have the next ping cross the threshhold
   - This makes the keep-alive ping take the `_writeLock`
4. Reconnect A before the `DisconnectTimeout` (default 15s) and drop it again.
**Observe** `_writeLock` remains held such that any send to A, including broadcasts that include A, do not complete

- On reconnect, [`UpdateConnectionPair`](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/70dc164847bb029321a3d0eea9b74db1fdb48055/src/SignalR/common/Http.Connections/src/Internal/HttpConnectionContext.cs#L1069) doesn't cancel the old pipe's pending flush or complete its old reader. It should cancel the pending flush and complete the old reader so that we're no longer waiting for the flush to complete (and holding `_writeLock` during it)
- Keep-alive pings don't observe connection termination. `TryWritePingAsync` has an existing TODO for cancellation
https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/70dc164847bb029321a3d0eea9b74db1fdb48055/src/SignalR/server/Core/src/HubConnectionContext.cs#L541-L552

Issues.Title: IIS in-process: response silently truncated after first flush when a System.Web module subscribes to PreSendRequestContent
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this? - [x] I have searched the existing issues ### Describe the bug An ASP.NET Core app hosted in-process under IIS (AspNetCoreModuleV2) returns `200 OK` with a body truncated at the first flush whenever a .NET Framework `IHttpModule` in the same pipeline subscribes to `HttpApplication.PreSendRequestContent`. The handler can be a no-op. No exception reaches application code, the status code is 200, and the chunked response is terminated cleanly, so clients just receive incomplete content (for example, unparseable JSON). The site is the only application in its app pool. The pool's .NET CLR version is `v4.0` (the IIS default), which the ASP.NET Core hosting docs allow even though "No Managed Code" is recommended. The other requirement is a managed module in the site's pipeline that subscribes to `PreSendRequestContent`. In the environment where we found this, neither piece came from the application's own code. A third-party module installed in the GAC (the kind typically registered server-wide, so every site inherits it) put System.Web into the Core application's pipeline. A second, unrelated third-party module, a monitoring/security agent, subscribed to `PreSendRequestContent`. Each was harmless alone. Application owners may not know CLR4 is loading at all. Reproduces on ASP.NET Core 10.0.14, 9.0.22, 9.0.0 and 8.0.33. It is deterministic, not a race. Every request is truncated. The first-chance exception in the worker process is a `NullReferenceException` in `AsyncIOEngine.NotifyCompletion`. The native flush completion is delivered re-entrantly, on the same thread, while `http_flush_response_bytes` is still on the stack. This first-chance stack was captured on .NET 8. The .NET 10 event log entry under "Exceptions" shows the same top frames. ``` System.NullReferenceException: Object reference not set to an instance of an object. at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.IO.AsyncIOEngine.NotifyCompletion(Int32 hr, Int32 bytes) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.IISHttpServer.OnAsyncCompletion(IntPtr pvManagedHttpContext, Int32 hr, Int32 bytes) --- managed to native transition --- at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.NativeMethods.http_flush_response_bytes(NativeSafeHandle, Boolean, Boolean&) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.NativeMethods.HttpFlushResponseBytes(NativeSafeHandle, Boolean, Boolean&) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.IO.AsyncIOEngine.AsyncFlushOperation.InvokeOperation(Int32&, Int32&) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.IO.AsyncIOOperation.Invoke() at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.IO.AsyncIOEngine.Run(AsyncIOOperation) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.IO.AsyncIOEngine.FlushAsync(Boolean) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.IISHttpContext.WriteBody(...) ... at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.IIS.Core.HttpResponseStream.WriteAsync(ReadOnlyMemory`1, CancellationToken) ``` **Analysis** `AsyncIOEngine.Run` (identical in `release/10.0` and `main`, and unchanged since .NET 8) calls `ioOperation.Invoke()` while `_runningOperation` is still `null`, and only assigns `_runningOperation` after `Invoke()` returns. https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/v10.0.14/src/Servers/IIS/IIS/src/Core/IO/AsyncIOEngine.cs#L175-L177 ```csharp lock (_context._contextLock) { ... var completed = ioOperation.Invoke() != null; if (!completed) { _runningOperation = ioOperation; } } ``` `NotifyCompletion` takes the same (re-entrant) lock and dereferences `_runningOperation`, guarded only by `Debug.Assert`. When IIS delivers the flush completion inline during `IHttpResponse::Flush`, the callback re-enters on the same thread, finds `_runningOperation == null`, and throws. `IISHttpServer.OnAsyncCompletion` catches it, logs "Unexpected exception in IISHttpServer.OnAsyncCompletion", and returns `RQ_NOTIFICATION_FINISH_REQUEST`. IIS then ends the response normally, which is why the client sees a well-formed 200 with a short body instead of an error. `http_flush_response_bytes` in the in-process handler passes `IHttpResponse::Flush(fAsync: TRUE, ...)` straight through, and `IN_PROCESS_HANDLER::AsyncCompletion` forwards to managed code without detecting re-entrancy. The inline completion appears to come from System.Web's (webengine4) handling of the send-response notification. A native module registered for `RQ_SEND_RESPONSE` does **not** trigger it, so the trigger is specific to managed `PreSendRequestContent`. Regardless of which IIS component delivers the completion inline, the managed engine could tolerate it, for example by recording the operation as running before calling `Invoke()` (or detecting a completion that arrives during `Invoke()`), and by not silently ending the response on failure. ### Expected Behavior The full response body is sent. If a flush genuinely fails, the request should fail visibly (for example, by aborting the connection) instead of completing as a 200 with a partial body. ### Steps To Reproduce Minimal repro: https://github.com/m0nkey653/aspnetcore-iis-presendrequestcontent-truncation It has two projects and a README with copy-paste steps. - `App`, a .NET 10 minimal API. `GET /` writes `first`, calls `FlushAsync()`, writes `second` and calls `FlushAsync()` again. - `PreSendModule`, a .NET Framework 4.8 `IHttpModule` whose only code is `app.PreSendRequestContent += (s, e) => { };`. It is registered in the app's `web.config` `` section with no `preCondition`, so it runs for requests handled by AspNetCoreModuleV2. Prerequisites are IIS with the ASP.NET 4.8 feature, the .NET 10 SDK and the .NET 10 Hosting Bundle. From an elevated PowerShell prompt in the repo root: ```powershell # 1. Publish the app, and build the module into the site's bin folder dotnet publish App -c Release -o C:\inetpub\PreSendRepro dotnet build PreSendModule -c Release -o C:\inetpub\PreSendRepro\bin # 2. App pool with .NET CLR v4.0 (the IIS default) and a site on port 8086 $appcmd = "$env:windir\System32\inetsrv\appcmd.exe" & $appcmd add apppool /name:PreSendRepro /managedRuntimeVersion:v4.0 /managedPipelineMode:Integrated & $appcmd add site /name:PreSendRepro /bindings:"http/*:8086:" /physicalPath:C:\inetpub\PreSendRepro & $appcmd set app "PreSendRepro/" /applicationPool:PreSendRepro # 3. Request the page, printing the body and then the status code curl.exe -s -w "%{http_code}`n" http://localhost:8086/ ``` Expected output is `first`, `second`, `200`. Actual output is `first`, `200`, on every request. Issues.Title: CacheView: second and later requests return HTTP 500 when a cached child declares @rendermode on its own type
Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this? I searched issues and PRs for `CacheView`, `CacheBoundary`, `IsCacheableComponent`, `CacheViewKeyResolver`, `SSRRenderModeBoundary`, `CacheBehavior`, `ThrowIfNestedInsideCapturingCacheView`, `"has a fixed rendermode"` and `InstantiateComponent CacheView`, open and closed, searching both the `rendermode` and `render-mode` spellings, and found nothing describing this. I also read the eight `[Validation]` issues that cover `CacheView`, #69119 through #69126, plus #69347. The string `500` does not appear in any of them, and `InvalidOperationException` appears only in #69121 (the `CacheKey` collision) and #69125 (the documented refusals). Two of those look like they already cover this, and I want to be explicit about why they don't, because the difference is one line of Razor: - **#69121** concludes that *"interactive render-mode boundaries work inside cached static content"*, with 4 Pass in its optional render-mode exploration. - **#69124** records a Documentation Pass quoting the public docs: *"antiforgery tokens and interactive render-mode boundaries render fresh on every request while surrounding content remains cached"*. Both are right, and I reproduce both results. They exercise the render mode supplied at the **call site** (``), which works on every request. What throws is the other spelling: the render mode declared **on the component's own type** (`@rendermode InteractiveServer` at the top of its `.razor`, i.e. a `[RenderModeAttribute]`). I could not find that case in any of the validation issues, and the two spellings are interchangeable everywhere else in Blazor, which is why I think this is worth filing. ### Describe the bug A component placed inside a `` whose render mode is declared **on its own type** (`@rendermode InteractiveServer` at the top of its `.razor`, i.e. a `[RenderModeAttribute]`) makes every cache **hit** throw an unhandled exception, so the first request succeeds and every later request returns HTTP 500 until the cache entry expires. The same component works when the render mode is supplied at the **call site** (``). That is the only difference. ``` System.InvalidOperationException: The component type 'minrepro.Components.Pages.Boom' has a fixed rendermode of 'Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Web.InteractiveServerRenderMode', so it is not valid to specify any rendermode when using this component. at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.ComponentFactory.InstantiateComponent(IServiceProvider serviceProvider, Type componentType, IComponentRenderMode callerSpecifiedRenderMode, Nullable`1 parentComponentId) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.RenderTree.Renderer.InstantiateChildComponentOnFrame(RenderTreeFrame[] frames, Int32 frameIndex, Int32 parentComponentId) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.RenderTree.RenderTreeDiffBuilder.InitializeNewComponentFrame(DiffContext& diffContext, Int32 frameIndex) ... at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Endpoints.EndpointHtmlRenderer.RenderEndpointComponent(HttpContext httpContext, Type rootComponentType, ParameterView parameters, Boolean waitForQuiescence) at Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.Endpoints.RazorComponentEndpointInvoker.RenderComponentCore(HttpContext context) ``` ### To Reproduce From scratch, no authentication, no extra packages: ```bash dotnet new blazor -o CacheViewRepro -f net11.0 -int Server cd CacheViewRepro ``` `Components/Pages/Boom.razor`: ```razor @rendermode InteractiveServer

interactive child, counter @count

@code { private int count; } ``` `Components/Pages/Repro.razor`: ```razor @page "/repro"

repro

cached content

 ``` Then: ```bash dotnet publish -c Release -o out ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production ASPNETCORE_URLS=http://127.0.0.1:5414 dotnet out/CacheViewRepro.dll & for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5414/repro -o /dev/null -w "request $i -> HTTP %{http_code}\n"; done ``` ### Observed ``` request 1 -> HTTP 200 request 2 -> HTTP 500 request 3 -> HTTP 500 ``` The default cache entry lifetime is 30 seconds (`DefaultCacheViewExpiration`), so requests start succeeding again once the entry expires, then fail again after the next one is created. ### Control, in the same app and the same process Add a second page whose child gets its render mode at the **call site** instead, so both spellings run side by side under one host: `Components/Pages/Calm.razor` (same component, without the `@rendermode` line): ```razor

interactive child, counter @count

@code { private int count; } ``` `Components/Pages/Control.razor`: ```razor @page "/control"

control

cached content

 ``` Four requests to each, same process, immediately after each other: ``` / -> HTTP 200 (sanity check) /control (render mode at the call site) request 1 -> HTTP 200 request 2 -> HTTP 200 request 3 -> HTTP 200 request 4 -> HTTP 200 /repro (render mode on the component type) request 1 -> HTTP 200 request 2 -> HTTP 500 request 3 -> HTTP 500 request 4 -> HTTP 500 ``` So it isn't the cache, the component, the interactivity or the host: the only variable is where the render mode is declared. ### Why this looks like a defect rather than an unsupported combination `ComponentFactory.InstantiateComponent` only throws when **both** a render mode on the type and a caller-specified render mode are present: ```csharp var effectiveRenderMode = callerSpecifiedRenderMode is null ? componentTypeRenderMode! : componentTypeRenderMode is null ? callerSpecifiedRenderMode : throw new InvalidOperationException($"The component type '{componentType}' has a fixed rendermode ..."); ``` In the repro the app supplies exactly **one** of them, the one on the type. The second is supplied by the framework on the cache-hit path, so the message asks the developer to remove a render mode they never wrote, and the suggested fix is not available to them. It also runs against an intent the framework states elsewhere: `SSRRenderModeBoundary` is annotated `[CacheBehavior(CacheBehavior.Rerender)]`, i.e. the boundary is meant to survive caching and re-render on each request. On the first request it does exactly that; on the second it throws. ### Expected Either the cached child is restored without re-applying a render mode to a type that already fixes one, or `CacheView` rejects the component up front the way it already rejects `AuthorizeView` and a nested `CacheView`, with a message naming the problem. An unhandled exception reaching Kestrel on every cache hit does not seem intended. ### Second, smaller point: the shipped XML documentation contradicts the Learn page The XML documentation shipped in the reference pack says: > `T:Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.CacheView` — "A component that caches the rendered HTML of > its child content during server-side rendering (SSR). **On cache hit, child components are not > instantiated or rendered.**" Measured on the cache-hit request, with a component that renders its render-mode state and logs from `OnInitializedAsync`, the child **is** instantiated on a cache hit — twice, once statically and once interactively — with the parameter values captured when the entry was created. That matches the Learn page, which says the opposite of the XML summary: > "Components marked with `CacheBehavior.Rerender` run their lifecycle on every request, but > their parameter values are captured when the cache entry is created and replayed unchanged on > cache hits." `SSRRenderModeBoundary` carries `[CacheBehavior(CacheBehavior.Rerender)]`, so the Learn wording is the accurate one. The XML summary is the text that shows up in IntelliSense, and read on its own it suggests that nothing inside a `CacheView` can capture per-request state — which is the opposite of the guidance the Learn page gives. Worth a one-line amendment. ### Coverage note, offered as data In case it is useful for a regression test alongside the fix, as of `main` today: - `src/Components/test/E2ETest/Tests/CacheViewTestBase.cs` — 236 lines, 10 `[Fact]`s (`CacheViewCachesData`, `CacheViewDoesNotCacheDataWhenNotEnabled`, `CacheViewCorrectlyCreatesLiveCachedComponents`, `EditFormWithFormComponents_CachesStaticContent_AndFormStillSubmits`, `CacheViewInLoopUsesVaryByForDistinctEntries`, `CacheViewMultipleLiveCachedComponentsOfSameType_PreserveCorrectOrder`, `CacheViewCachesHardcodedLiveCachedComponent`, `CacheViewTreatsStreamingChildAsLiveCachedComponent`, `CacheViewServesCachedContentToHeadRequests`, `CacheViewPopulatedByHeadRequest_IsServedToLaterGetRequest`). Zero occurrences of `rendermode`. - `src/Components/Endpoints/test/IsCacheableComponentTest.cs` — 96 lines, 7 `[Fact]`s, all about the presence and matching of `[CacheBehavior]` / `[CacheCondition]`. `SSRRenderModeBoundary` is not named in it. ### Further technical details - `Microsoft.AspNetCore.App` **11.0.0-rc.3.26522.148**, SDK **11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148** - Linux x64, Kestrel, `ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production` - Stock `dotnet new blazor -f net11.0 -int Server` template, two files added, no packages added - Default `CacheView` store (`MemoryCacheViewStore`); no `HybridCache` registered - Raised before GA since it is cheaper to fix in an RC

# Prototype reference-backed cancellation parameters in JSInterop

<!-- Thank you for submitting a pull request to our repo. -->

<!-- If this is your first PR in the ASP.NET Core repo, please run through the checklist
below to ensure a smooth review and merge process for your PR. -->

- [x] You've read the [Contributor Guide](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) and [Code of Conduct](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/main/CODE-OF-CONDUCT.md).
- [x] You've included unit or integration tests for your change, where applicable.
- [x] You've included inline docs for your change, where applicable.
- [x] There's an open issue for the PR that you are making. If you'd like to propose a new feature or change, please open an issue to discuss the change or find an existing issue.

<!-- Once all that is done, you're ready to go. Open the PR with the content below. -->

Project cancellation parameter values through existing object references.

## Description

**Revised experimental draft: this replaces the original invocation-cancellation design.** Cancellation is an ordinary parameter value in both directions, not an operation mode. Specification: #70326. API proposal: #70327. Replacement commit: ec33043d48. No API approval or shipping readiness is claimed.

### Consumer shape

JavaScript supplies a signal-backed reference to an ordinary CancellationToken argument. The token need not be last:

```javascript
const reference = await dotNetObject.createCancellationTokenReference(controller.signal);
try {
    const result = await dotNetObject.invokeMethodAsync("Load", reference, query);
} finally {
    await reference.disposeAsync();
}
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public Task<SearchResult> Load(CancellationToken cancellationToken, string query);
```

.NET supplies a token-backed reference to an ordinary JavaScript AbortSignal argument:

```csharp
await using var reference =
    await DotNetCancellationTokenReference.CreateAsync(jsRuntime, cancellationToken);
await jsRuntime.InvokeVoidAsync("receiveSignal", reference);
```

JavaScript receives a **native AbortSignal**, suitable for `fetch(url, { signal })`. The application decides whether to observe or ignore it. Keep the owner alive if the receiver retains the token/signal after returning; references can span multiple invocations.

### What changed

- Remove `invokeMethodAsyncWithCancellation`, final-token injection, the cancellation argument envelope, reserved cancel invocation, per-runtime call-ID cancellation registry, and special promise rejection/completion cleanup.
- Wrap the JavaScript signal subscription in a JSObjectReference and the managed cancellation source in a DotNetObjectReference. A CancellationToken converter unwraps the source in an ordinary argument slot.
- Add `DotNetCancellationTokenReference.CreateAsync` as an explicit outgoing owner. It holds a managed token observer through DotNetObjectReference and a native signal through JSObjectReference; serialization delegates to the existing reference converter.
- Use async reference factories so bridge setup and pre-cancel state are established before passing values. The object-bound JS factory uses that object's dispatcher; the global `DotNet.createCancellationTokenReference` variant remains available for an unambiguous default runtime.
- Make disposal reference-owned and idempotent. Incoming cleanup detaches the listener, waits outstanding notification/callback work, and releases both references. Outgoing cleanup ends observation and waits for JS before revoking references. Neither requests cancellation, aborts an uncanceled signal, or disposes the caller's source/controller.
- Preserve ordinary invocation results/errors and the existing InvokeAsync control-token behavior. An ignoring handler stays pending and can complete normally; a handler can catch cancellation and return normally. A pre-aborted input still invokes .NET with a canceled token.
- Add XML docs and PublicAPI.Unshipped entries for the new .NET reference surface; revise the existing API proposal instead of filing another issue.

The outgoing bridge retains an ordinary observation promise and token registration until cancellation/disposal. This is a resource of the reference, not a policy applied to the user's operation. Raw outgoing token serialization requires the explicit owner so its lifetime is not hidden.

### Validation

Final runs on Windows/Chromium: **182 managed tests passed** (12 new reference cases, every Boolean row inspected), and **22 browser tests passed**: ten new shared scenarios plus the existing ordinary-interop control in each of Server and WebAssembly. Both runtime cells were observed independently.

Coverage includes both mappings; non-final token argument position; independent references; cancellation handled with a normal result; ignored cancellation without forced promise settlement; pre-aborted input still invoking the method; retention/reuse after return; native signal identity/type and pre-canceled fetch; normal failure preserving the reference lifetime; disposal without cancellation; and the invocation control token not aborting a separate signal or stopping JavaScript.

Exact final commands, from the worktree root (`. .\activate.ps1` before dotnet; tests used `ASPNETCORE_TEST_LOG_MAXPATH=32767`):

```powershell
# Passed: standalone package declarations
node_modules\.bin\tsc.cmd --build src\Components\Web.JS\JSInterop\tsconfig.json --pretty false

# Passed: no lint errors
node_modules\.bin\eslint.cmd -c src\Components\Web.JS\src\.eslintrc.js src\Components\Web.JS\src\JSInterop\Microsoft.JSInterop.ts --quiet

# Passed: Debug and Release browser bundles
Push-Location src\Components\Web.JS; npm run build; Pop-Location

# Passed: 182 tests
dotnet test src\Components\JSInterop\test\Microsoft.JSInterop.Tests.csproj --no-restore -v:q -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:GenerateInstallers=false --logger 'console;verbosity=normal'

# Passed: 0 warnings, 0 errors
dotnet build src\Components\test\E2ETest\Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj --no-restore -v:q -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:GenerateInstallers=false

# Passed: 22 tests, 11 per runtime
dotnet test src\Components\test\E2ETest\Microsoft.AspNetCore.Components.E2ETests.csproj --no-build --no-restore -v:q -p:UseIisNativeAssets=false -p:GenerateInstallers=false --filter 'FullyQualifiedName~InteropCancellationTest|FullyQualifiedName~InteropTest.CanInvokeInteropMethods' --logger 'console;verbosity=normal'
```

**Negative controls:** temporarily disabling incoming source cancellation and returning false for outgoing cancellation made the retained-token managed check and canceled observer row fail with expected true/actual false; the None control stayed green. On BOTH Server and WebAssembly, the identical native-signal-after-return assertion failed with expected `aborted in JS`/actual `native signal retained`; pre-canceled fetch controls remained green. Restoring forwarding made all final suites green.

A canonical per-page Server sample was exercised in a real browser before selecting permanent tests, then removed after permanent coverage passed. It demonstrated both projections, a normal result after handling cancellation, and a native signal reacting after call return. No observed errors/failed resources during the final probe; sample servers stopped. Architecture and final fresh-context correctness/test-validity reviews completed with no significant final findings within scope.

### Remaining design questions and unverified boundaries

- Names/placement of the reference factories and public framework callback surface require API review. PublicAPI.Unshipped tracks compatibility, not approval. The proposal is updated for the final implemented shape.
- Factories/disposal require cross-runtime calls; no benchmark is claimed. Callers must explicitly keep owners alive and dispose them. Abort events cannot await transport, so event notification failures are logged and retained for disposal to observe, not applied as a new invocation outcome.
- Browser abort reasons are not translated into .NET exceptions. Cancellation is cooperative; no automatic operation cancellation, work rollback, service disposal or implicit app/component lifetime policy is added.
- WebView, Native AOT/trimming publish, multithreaded WebAssembly, actual mixed-runtime E2E, Auto transitions, reconnect/resume and non-Chromium browsers remain unverified. The object-bound factory selects its runtime, but simultaneous mixed-runtime E2E has not been run. Static SSR/prerender have no JS interop.
- Expected JSDisconnectedException cleanup follows existing object-reference conventions; broader disconnected-runtime policy remains experimental. Installer validation is not claimed.

Keep this PR **draft**. No ready state, merge or auto-merge is requested. The work remains independent of AI.Mcp changes and contains no MCP dependency.

Issues.Body:
<!--
This template is useful to build consensus about whether work should be done, and if so, the high-level shape of how it should be approached. Use this before fixating on a particular implementation.
-->

## Summary

This document proposes bidirectional, reference-owned projections between browser AbortSignal values and .NET CancellationToken parameters in JSInterop. Cancellation is an ordinary argument value, not an invocation mode. Existing interop methods retain their result, failure and control-token semantics.

This replaces the initial invocation-cancellation experiment. There is no new cancellable-invocation API, call-ID cancellation registry, argument envelope, reserved cancel message or promise-rejection policy.

## Motivation and goals

1. Let an ordinary JSInvokable signature declare a CancellationToken parameter, with JavaScript supplying a referenced AbortSignal projection in that argument position.
2. Let .NET supply a referenced token projection to JavaScript functions that accept native AbortSignal values, including browser APIs such as fetch.
3. Give cancellation values explicit lifetimes independent of any one invocation, so a receiver can retain and reuse them after a call returns.
4. Preserve operation ownership: the receiver chooses whether to observe cancellation, ignore it, catch it or use it for later work.
5. Reuse JSObjectReference and DotNetObjectReference transport and release their listeners, registrations and references explicitly.

## In scope

- Ordinary CancellationToken arguments supplied by JavaScript signal references.
- Native AbortSignal arguments supplied by .NET token references.
- Retention/reuse after invocation return, pre-cancel, independent references, normal completion/failure, ignored cancellation, and explicit cleanup without cancellation.
- Separate managed-wait control-token semantics; Server and WebAssembly validation.

## Out of scope

1. Automatically cancel an interop invocation, reject its promise, skip a method for a pre-canceled input or undo work.
2. Reinterpret the existing CancellationToken controlling IJSRuntime.InvokeAsync as an argument or browser signal.
3. Serialize token/controller state as ordinary JSON, transfer AbortController authority to the other runtime or project arbitrary JavaScript abort reasons into .NET exceptions.
4. Automatically infer cancellation-value lifetime from method completion, component lifetime or source disposal.
5. Claim complete coverage of WebView, Native AOT/trimming, multithreaded WebAssembly, multiple runtimes, Auto transitions or circuit reconnect/resumption.

## Risks / unknowns

This is an experimental proposal, not API approval. The previous call-level cancellation design is superseded. Factory/type names and framework callback placement require API review. Owners must be disposed explicitly; the outgoing bridge retains a registration and ordinary pending observation until cancellation/disposal. Abort events cannot await transport, so notification failures are reported to the console and observed by disposal. No benchmark is claimed. WebView, Native AOT/trimming publish, multithreaded WebAssembly, actual mixed runtimes, Auto transitions, reconnect/resume and non-Chromium remain unverified. The object-bound JS factory selects its runtime; the global variant requires the existing unambiguous default dispatcher.

## Examples

Provide explicitly owned reference factories. JavaScript wraps its signal using `dotNetObject.createCancellationTokenReference(signal)` and passes the returned reference as an ordinary argument in that object's runtime. `DotNet.createCancellationTokenReference(signal)` is also available when there is one unambiguous default runtime. The receiving .NET parameter is declared CancellationToken and can appear in any ordinary parameter position. .NET uses `DotNetCancellationTokenReference.CreateAsync(jsRuntime, token)` and passes that reference as an ordinary argument; JavaScript receives a native AbortSignal.

Owners dispose the references only when the receiving side no longer needs the value. Disposal ends observation and releases bridge resources; it does not request cancellation or dispose the original token source/controller. Creation is asynchronous because references and subscriptions must be established across the runtime boundary.

### JS signal to .NET token

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const reference = await dotNetObject.createCancellationTokenReference(controller.signal);
try {
    const result = await dotNetObject.invokeMethodAsync("Load", reference, query);
} finally {
    await reference.disposeAsync();
}
```

```csharp
[JSInvokable]
public Task<SearchResult> Load(CancellationToken cancellationToken, string query);
```

SearchResult is the application's existing serializable result. The application does not implement a cancellation-source registry or Cancel endpoint. The token is not injected out-of-band and need not be last.

### .NET token to native JS signal

```csharp
await using var reference =
    await DotNetCancellationTokenReference.CreateAsync(jsRuntime, cancellationToken);
await jsRuntime.InvokeVoidAsync("receiveSignal", reference);
```

```javascript
function receiveSignal(signal) {
    return fetch("/data", { signal });
}
```

The JavaScript value is a native AbortSignal suitable for browser APIs. It is not a JSON token, DotNetObject wrapper or special cancellable promise. The underlying application operation, not interop, controls how the signal affects it.

### Already canceled inputs

An already-aborted JavaScript signal still permits invocation of .NET: the method starts with a canceled token and can return a normal result. A pre-canceled .NET token produces an already-aborted native signal before the JavaScript function begins; fetch rejects it through fetch's own semantics.

### Running cancellation and independent values

Aborting a JavaScript controller cancels its projected .NET token. Canceling a .NET source aborts the projected browser signal. Different reference owners are independent. Several calls can deliberately share one reference, and several references can deliberately observe one original token or signal.

### No forced operation or promise outcome

A handler that ignores its token remains pending until its own work ends and can then complete normally. A handler that catches cancellation can return a normal result. Normal handler exceptions remain ordinary interop errors. Cancellation does not impose a new framework promise-settlement policy.

### Lifetime past method return

A .NET method can retain a supplied token and observe cancellation after returning. A JavaScript function can retain a native signal and observe abort after returning. The owner keeps the reference alive for that interval. Invocation completion or failure does not release it.

An incoming reference can be reused in another ordinary invocation. An outgoing reference produces the same native signal while its owner remains alive. Do not reuse a disposed owner.

### Explicit cleanup

Incoming disposal removes the abort listener, coordinates any in-progress cancellation notification, disposes the owned managed source and releases JS/.NET references. It does not cancel a retained token that was previously uncanceled.

Outgoing disposal stops the managed token registration, completes its observation without requesting abort, waits for the JavaScript observer to finish, and releases both references. It does not cancel the original source or abort an uncanceled browser signal.

Disposal is idempotent. Owners must still dispose references when their application operation fails. Expected disconnected-browser cleanup follows existing JSDisconnectedException handling; general reconnect/resume behavior remains unverified.

### Invocation control token remains distinct

The CancellationToken parameter controlling `IJSRuntime.InvokeAsync` still cancels only the managed wait. It does not become an AbortSignal and does not stop the JavaScript function. A separately supplied reference argument continues observing its own token. Canceling one does not cancel the other.

### Failure reporting and extensibility

Reference creation and disposal are awaitable and report failures. An abort event cannot await transport, so asynchronous incoming notification failures are reported to the browser console and retained for disposal to observe. Cancellation callback failures do not silently become successful cancellation. Outgoing observation failures are likewise reported and remain observable through disposal.

The factories return explicit owners rather than defining extensible transports or policy interfaces. Raw outgoing token serialization is rejected with guidance to create an owner; otherwise its reference lifetime would be undefined.

## Assumptions

- Browser AbortSignal and AbortController are available. No polyfill or browser reason-to-exception mapping is included.
- Receivers cooperate if they want cancellation. Projection alone cannot interrupt work.
- Reference factories require an available, connected JS runtime; static SSR/prerendering cannot use them.
- Matched JavaScript/.NET framework assets and existing object-reference ownership rules apply.
- Callers explicitly dispose owners when receivers no longer need the value, not necessarily when a call completes.
- Server and WebAssembly are evaluated separately. Passing one runtime does not establish other host/lifecycle cells.
- Public factory names and placement, infrastructure callback surface, creation overhead and disconnect policy remain API/design review questions.

## Experiment and validation

This replaces the original invocation-level experiment in the same draft PR, not an additional cancellation protocol. Implementation: #70328. Separate API proposal: #70327. The reference types are now recorded in PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt; no API approval is claimed.

The implementation uses only ordinary object-reference interop. The incoming JS subscription owner has a JSObjectReference; its managed source has a DotNetObjectReference. A CancellationToken converter unwraps that source in an ordinary argument slot. The outgoing owner has a managed token observer and a referenced native browser signal; its converter delegates to existing JSObjectReference serialization. There is no invocation-ID cancellation registry, special argument envelope, reserved cancel message or framework-driven promise rejection. Creation and disposal are explicit cross-runtime operations, not operation policy.

Issues.Title: SignalR: keep-alive ping and stateful reconnect ack race on Transport.Output, corrupting the stream
Issues.Body:
Is there an existing issue for this?

I searched the issues and found nothing matching. PR #65732 touches MessageBuffer write cancellation but not this race.

Describe the bug

With stateful reconnect on, the server can write a keep-alive ping and a stateful reconnect AckMessage to the same PipeWriter at the same time. Each writer holds a different lock, so nothing serializes them. The bytes mix on the wire, and the client fails to parse the stream and drops the connection.

The two writers in release/10.0:

Writer | Lock held | Writes to -- | -- | -- HubConnectionContext.TryWritePingAsync / TryWritePingSlowAsync (HubConnectionContext.cs) | HubConnectionContext._writeLock | _connectionContext.Transport.Output MessageBuffer.RunTimer (MessageBuffer.cs), every AckRate (1 s) when _lastAckedId < _latestReceivedSequenceId | MessageBuffer._writeLock | _writer, set from connection.Transport.Output in the constructor

Normal hub messages are safe: HubConnectionContext.WriteCore calls _messageBuffer.WriteAsync while holding HubConnectionContext._writeLock, and MessageBuffer then takes its own lock. But the ping path never takes MessageBuffer._writeLock, and the ack timer never takes HubConnectionContext._writeLock. The ping path doesn't check UsingStatefulReconnect() either, so it bypasses the buffer.

The window opens when the server has sent nothing for KeepAliveInterval, so a ping is due, while the client keeps sending messages that need an ack, for example the reply to a long-running server-to-client request.

Expected behavior

Pings and acks are serialized with each other and with normal hub messages, so the stream stays well formed.

Steps to reproduce

We have no minimal repro yet. Observed setup:

  • ASP.NET Core server hub with AllowStatefulReconnects = true, KeepAliveInterval = 8 s, ClientTimeoutInterval = 17.6 s, JSON protocol.
  • .NET client (Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client 10.0.13) with .WithStatefulReconnect(), .WithAutomaticReconnect(...), WithKeepAliveInterval(8 s), WithServerTimeout(17.6 s), WebSockets transport over localhost.
  • The server calls client methods through IHubContext<T>.Clients.All.SendCoreAsync, and the client replies by invoking a hub method.
  • The connection drops 10 to 15 times a day at irregular times. We are shipping a build with stateful reconnect off and will report whether the drops stop.

A repro would likely need a server that sends nothing while the client invokes hub methods often, with a short KeepAliveInterval to make collisions more frequent.

Exceptions (if any)

Client side, raised as HubConnection.Reconnecting. The first character changes from drop to drop: 's', 'o', and an empty message.

System.IO.InvalidDataException: Error reading JSON.
 ---> System.Text.Json.JsonReaderException: 's' is an invalid start of a value. LineNumber: 0 | BytePositionInLine: 0.
   at System.Text.Json.ThrowHelper.ThrowJsonReaderException(Utf8JsonReader& json, ExceptionResource resource, Byte nextByte, ReadOnlySpan`1 bytes)
   at System.Text.Json.Utf8JsonReader.ConsumeValue(Byte marker)
   at System.Text.Json.Utf8JsonReader.ReadFirstToken(Byte first)
   at System.Text.Json.Utf8JsonReader.ReadSingleSegment()
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Protocol.JsonHubProtocol.ParseMessage(ReadOnlySequence`1 input, IInvocationBinder binder)
   --- End of inner exception stack trace ---
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Protocol.JsonHubProtocol.ParseMessage(ReadOnlySequence`1 input, IInvocationBinder binder)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client.HubConnection.ReceiveLoop(ConnectionState connectionState)

System.IO.InvalidDataException: Error reading JSON.
 ---> System.Text.Json.JsonReaderException: The input does not contain any JSON tokens. Expected the input to start with a valid JSON token, when isFinalBlock is true. LineNumber: 0 | BytePositionInLine: 0.
   at System.Text.Json.ThrowHelper.ThrowJsonReaderException(Utf8JsonReader& json, ExceptionResource resource, Byte nextByte, ReadOnlySpan`1 bytes)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Protocol.JsonHubProtocol.ParseMessage(ReadOnlySequence`1 input, IInvocationBinder binder)
   --- End of inner exception stack trace ---
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Protocol.JsonHubProtocol.ParseMessage(ReadOnlySequence`1 input, IInvocationBinder binder)
   at Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client.HubConnection.ReceiveLoop(ConnectionState connectionState)

The server logs only a normal disconnect, with no exception.

.NET Version

  • Server: Microsoft.AspNetCore.App 10.0.14, Windows, Kestrel.
  • Client: Microsoft.AspNetCore.SignalR.Client 10.0.13, net10.0.

Anything else?

Possible fixes: have the ack timer take HubConnectionContext._writeLock, for example by passing that lock into MessageBuffer. Or, when stateful reconnect is on, route pings through MessageBuffer under its lock.

We haven't checked whether the .NET client has the same ping and ack pattern in the other direction.

Workaround: turn off stateful reconnect.

Issues.Title: JsonPatch: allow test operations against null and empty-string values
Issues.Body:
## Behavior before 
[{
     "op": "test",
     "path": "/name",
     "value": null 
}]
applied to `{ "name": null }` fails with "The value at 'name' cannot be null or empty to perform the test operation." ## Behavior after The same patch succeeds. `test` with `null` against a non-null value, or a non-null value against `null`, fails with "The current value '...' at path 'name' is not equal to the test value '...'." ## Description The `test` operation rejects a target whose current value is `null` (JSON object and dictionary adapters) or an empty string (JSON object adapters) before comparing anything, and reports "The value at '{0}' cannot be null or empty to perform the test operation." This affects both `Microsoft.AspNetCore.JsonPatch` and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.JsonPatch.SystemTextJson`. [RFC 6902 section 4.6 defines ](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc6902/#section-4.6)`test` as a pure equality check and lists `null` among the literals that compare equal when they are the same; empty strings compare equal under the string rule. A client that follows the spec and sends `{"op":"test","path":"/name","value":null}` before replacing a field that is still unset gets a failed patch instead of the optimistic-concurrency check it asked for. The guard is also inconsistent inside the library: `PocoAdapter` and `ListAdapter` compare null values normally, so the same patch succeeds or fails depending on whether the path resolves through a POCO, a dictionary or a `JsonObject`/`JObject`. This change removes the guard from `JObjectAdapter`, `JsonObjectAdapter` and both `DictionaryAdapter` implementations, so `test` falls through to the existing deep-equality comparison. A `null` target now matches a `null` test value, and a mismatch is reported with the existing "is not equal to the test value" message. The now unused `ValueForTargetSegmentCannotBeNullOrEmpty` resource is removed from both packages. #28021 already relaxed the dictionary adapter for empty strings in 2020; this finishes the job for `null` and for the JSON object adapters, which the System.Text.Json port inherited. #28019 reported the original problem and was closed as a duplicate of #25942, which is a different bug. * Fixes #28019 (not sure if I should open a copy when this was closed in error.) ## Nullable coercion in the Newtonsoft adapters Copilot's review pointed out that, with the guard gone, the Newtonsoft dictionary adapter accepted a `test` with `""` against a `null` `int?` entry. The cause is `ConversionResultProvider`: it round-trips the test value through Newtonsoft.Json into the target type, and Newtonsoft reads an empty string as `null` for a `Nullable` (`int?`, `bool?`, `DateTime?` and the other nullable primitives). The converted `null` then matched the `null` entry. The `PocoAdapter` and `ListAdapter` share the same helper and had no null guard, so they already behaved this way on `main`. The second commit makes the three Newtonsoft adapters compare the original test value instead of the converted one when the current value is `null`, so `null` only matches `null`. The System.Text.Json package is not affected: `JsonSerializer` refuses to convert `""` to a nullable primitive, so the conversion step fails and the test is rejected before the comparison. `test` against a `null` current value, Newtonsoft package: | Target | Test value | `main` | After first commit | After this PR | |---|---|---|---|---| | `JObject` property | `null` | fails: cannot be null or empty | succeeds | succeeds | | `JObject` property | `""` | fails: cannot be null or empty | fails: not equal | fails: not equal | | `Dictionary` entry | `null` | fails: cannot be null or empty | succeeds | succeeds | | `Dictionary` entry | `""` | fails: cannot be null or empty | **succeeds (wrong)** | fails: not equal | | `List` element | `null` | succeeds | succeeds | succeeds | | `List` element | `""` | **succeeds (wrong)** | **succeeds (wrong)** | fails: not equal | | POCO `int?`, `bool?`, `DateTime?` property | `null` | succeeds | succeeds | succeeds | | POCO `int?`, `bool?`, `DateTime?` property | `""` | **succeeds (wrong)** | **succeeds (wrong)** | fails: not equal | | POCO `string` property | `""` | fails: not equal | fails: not equal | fails: not equal | In the System.Text.Json package every `""`-against-`null` row fails with an invalid value error on `main` and after this PR, and every `null`-against-`null` row that failed on `main` now succeeds. ## Tests Added to both test projects: - `JsonPatchDocumentJObjectTest`: `test` against `null` and `""` succeeds, and mismatches in either direction throw `JsonPatchException` with the equality error message. - `DictionaryAdapterTest`: `TryTest` with a `null` dictionary value succeeds for a `null` test value and fails for a non-null one, and vice versa. - `DictionaryIntegrationTest`: end-to-end `JsonPatchDocument.Test` against a `null` dictionary entry. - `ExpandoObjectIntegrationTest` (Newtonsoft only): the null counterparts of the existing empty-string tests. Both test projects pass locally with `./eng/build.sh -test -projects ` (247 and 290 tests).

Issues.Title: Template `pr-docs-check` as a reusable gh-aw shared component for other dotnet repos
Issues.Body:
`pr-docs-check` (our gh-aw workflow that analyzes merged PRs and opens draft documentation PRs in `dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs`) was recently copied wholesale into `dotnet/runtime` ([[dotnet/runtime#135973](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/135973)](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/135973)), including its workflow frontmatter, prompt body, and Python helper scripts. This works, but it means every consumer repo maintains its own full copy — bug fixes and security hardening made in one place don't propagate to the others, and `runtime`'s copy already lacks a CI runner for its ported test suite.


gh-aw already has first-class support for exactly this scenario via cross-repo `imports:` with a typed `import-schema` parameter contract (see [[Sharing Workflows in the Organization](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/guides/sharing-workflows/)](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/guides/sharing-workflows/) and [[Imports Reference](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/imports/)](https://github.github.com/gh-aw/reference/imports/)). We should restructure `pr-docs-check` to use it.


## Goal


Extract the generic, repo-agnostic logic of `pr-docs-check` into a shared, versioned gh-aw component that `dotnet/aspnetcore` itself consumes (dogfooding) and that other repos (`dotnet/runtime`, `dotnet/aspire`, etc.) can install via `imports:` + `with:` parameters instead of copy-pasting the whole workflow.


## Classification of what moves where


**Generic (goes into the shared component):**



- Trigger/authorization gating pattern (`workflow_dispatch`/`pull_request_target` manual-rollout shape, bot/role allowlist).

- Credential-separation pattern (GitHub App token for checkout/tools/safe-outputs, separate head-repo app token for the automation fork, `min-integrity: merged`).

- Safe-outputs job shape: `create-pull-request` / `push-to-pull-request-branch` / `update-pull-request` / `notify-source-pr`, with `protected-files: blocked`, `draft: true`, `allowed-branches`, `required-title-prefix`.

- `find_existing_draft.py` duplicate-draft detection (already takes repo names as CLI args — low-cost to extract).

- `validate_outcome.py` safe-output preflight/postflight validator (needs an audit pass for any hardcoded `aspnetcore`/`AspNetCore.Docs` strings first).

- The generic prompt skeleton ("analyze PR, classify confidence tier, draft doc changes, push via safe outputs, notify source PR").



**Stays per-consumer (passed in as `import-schema` params or kept as consumer-owned files):**



- Source repo, docs target repo, docs automation/fork repo names.

- GitHub App secret names.

- Branch prefix, PR title prefix, labels, `allowed-files` glob (depends on the target docs repo's folder layout).

- `resolve_target_version.py` + `version-policy.json` — version/moniker resolution is inherently per-product (different release cadence/moniker scheme), so each consumer keeps its own.

- Product-specific prompt guidance (doc-structure conventions, breaking-change taxonomy wording for that product).



## Proposed shape


YAML






```
# shared/docs-check-core.md (no 'on:', shared component only)
import-schema:
  source-repository: { type: string, required: true }
  docs-target-repo:  { type: string, required: true }
  docs-head-repo:    { type: string, required: true }
  docs-app-client-id-secret:   { type: string, required: true }
  docs-app-private-key-secret: { type: string, required: true }
  branch-prefix:      { type: string, default: "docs/pr-" }
  title-prefix:        { type: string, default: "[docs] " }
  allowed-files-glob:  { type: string, required: true }

```





Consumers (including our own, refactored `pr-docs-check.md`) become a thin wrapper:


YAML






```
imports:
  - uses: <shared-repo>/shared/docs-check-core.md@v1
    with:
      source-repository: dotnet/aspnetcore
      docs-target-repo: dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs
      docs-head-repo: dotnet/AspNetCore.Docs.Automation
      ...

```





## Open design questions



1. Hosting location for the shared component: a new dedicated repo (e.g. `dotnet/agentic-workflows`) vs. a `shared/` folder inside `aspnetcore` that other repos import cross-repo from. A dedicated repo gives cleaner ownership/governance for cross-org consumers; a folder in `aspnetcore` is less setup but ties runtime's dependency to aspnetcore's branch/CI policy.

2. Versioning/ownership model once another repo (`runtime`) depends on the shared core — who reviews/approves changes, and do we pin consumers to a moving major ref (`@v1`) or exact tags?

3. Whether to also offer a generic "parse `Versions.props` + enumerate `release/*` branches" helper in the shared repo, vs. keeping version-policy resolution fully consumer-owned as proposed above.



## Proposed rollout order



1. Refactor/parameterize in place inside `aspnetcore` first; confirm `gh aw compile --strict` and existing `test_*` suites still pass.

2. Stand up the shared location, move the parameterized core there, tag `v1`.

3. Switch `aspnetcore`'s own `pr-docs-check.md` to consume the shared template via `imports:` (dogfood), validate with `gh aw trial`/manual dispatch before relying on it in production.

4. Once stable, open a follow-up PR to `dotnet/runtime` replacing its copy-pasted #135973 workflow with the `imports:` form — this also closes the "no CI for ported tests" gap flagged in that review, since tests now live once in the shared repo with their own test-running workflow.



## Validation



- `gh aw compile --validate --strict --zizmor` on both the shared component and each consumer's thin wrapper.

- Re-run existing Python/JS test suites against the extracted core.

- `gh aw trial ./pr-docs-check.md --host-repo <sandbox>` per consumer before enabling automatic triggers.

Refine `review-candidate-verifier` rules for external triggers and test gaps.

## Description

Refines `.github/agents/review-candidate-verifier.agent.md` (and the synchronized inline profile in `.github/workflows/pull-request-review.md`) to prevent false-positive `KEEP` verdicts on unbundled external-library triggers, speculative test-gap remedies, and pre-existing collaborator validation failures without losing valid behavioral findings.

### What changed
1. **Unbundled external triggers vs. caller-supplied extension hooks (#70232)**:
   - When `trigger` depends on the internal behavior of a concrete third-party package or runtime library method whose source/contract is not in the frozen bundle (as opposed to a caller-supplied implementation of a public interface or extension hook), `trigger` is unestablished and the verifier returns `DOWNGRADE` (`downgradeKind: "external"`).
2. **Test-gap consequence/remedy verification and no claim substitution (#70233)**:
   - For test-gap claims, `effect` requires verifying both that the test passes when the production fix is reverted and that the candidate's stated production consequence and prescribed assertion hold (failing before the fix and passing with it), without substituting an unstated bug or remedy to keep a candidate.
3. **Pre-existing collaborator guard failures and secondary-failure suppression (`#70043` r2 / #70269)**:
   - Marks `oldVsNew` contradicted (`DROP`, `contradictedLink: "oldVsNew"`) when `mergeBase` already triggers the same guard/validation failure in the underlying collaborator on the exact input sequence and only continued because an enclosing callback or persistence catch logged an error and omitted the required state/token.
   - Requires `contract` (from repository guidance or target-base code) before keeping a claim that a `catch` block suppressing a secondary diagnostic/cleanup failure while preserving the primary failure is a defect (`oldVsNew: "n/a"` when the primary failure already occurred at `mergeBase`).

Issues.Body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Describe the bug

With `EnableRequestDelegateGenerator`, query binding differs from the runtime path in three cases:

| Request | Runtime | RDG |
|---|---|---|
| `int x`, `?x=` | 400, `Failed to bind parameter "int x" from "".` | 200, `x` is 0 |
| `int? x`, `?x=abc` | 400, `Failed to bind parameter "Nullable<int> x" from "abc".` | 400 with no body, no exception, no log |
| `Guid[] x`, `?x=` | 400, `Failed to bind parameter "Guid[] x" from "".` | 200, `x` is `[00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000000]` |

A required value binds silently, and a parse failure on a nullable value skips `ThrowOnBadRequest` and the binding-failure log (#46362), so the client can't tell which parameter was wrong.

### Expected Behavior

RDG returns the same 400 as the runtime path, and throws the same `BadHttpRequestException` when `ThrowOnBadRequest` is on.

### Steps To Reproduce

Save as `repro.cs` and run `dotnet run repro.cs`:

```csharp
#:sdk Microsoft.NET.Sdk.Web
#:property EnableRequestDelegateGenerator=true

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Diagnostics;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateSlimBuilder(args);
builder.Services.Configure<RouteHandlerOptions>(options => options.ThrowOnBadRequest = true);
var app = builder.Build();
app.UseExceptionHandler(failed => failed.Run(context =>
    context.Response.WriteAsync(context.Features.Get<IExceptionHandlerFeature>()!.Error.Message)));

app.MapGet("/required", (int x) => x.ToString());
app.MapGet("/nullable", (int? x) => x?.ToString() ?? "null");
app.MapGet("/array", (Guid[] x) => string.Join(",", x));

app.Run();
```

```
curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:5000/required?x='
curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:5000/nullable?x=abc'
curl -s -w ' [%{http_code}]\n' 'localhost:5000/array?x='
```

Set `EnableRequestDelegateGenerator=false` and run again: each request returns a 400 that names `x`.

### Exceptions (if any)

None, in all three cases RDG throws nothing, with `ThrowOnBadRequest` on.

### .NET Version

11.0.100-rc.3.26522.148

### Anything else?

_No response_

Stop a JsonPatch `move` from adding the value when the removal fails

## Description

`ObjectAdapter.Move` called the private `Remove` for `from` and then always called `Add` for `path`. `Remove` reports failures through the error callback and returned `void`, so `Move` couldn't tell the removal failed. Without a callback the default reporter throws, so this only shows up when an error callback is passed (for example MVC's `ApplyTo(model, ModelState)`): the move is reported as an error but still applied as a copy.

The private `Remove` now returns `bool` and `Move` returns early when it fails. Same change in `Microsoft.AspNetCore.JsonPatch` and `Microsoft.AspNetCore.JsonPatch.SystemTextJson`.

Added a test to each package that moves from a get-only property with an error callback and checks that a single error is reported and the target property is left unchanged. Both tests fail without the change. Ran the JsonPatch and JsonPatch.SystemTextJson test projects locally (net12.0 and net472), all passing.

Fixes #69904

## Description

The review of #69445 saw the empty-catch feedback but deduplicated it and accepted preservation of the original processing error as justification for swallowing a separate logger failure. These are different policies: source and new tests can establish the implementation's intent without establishing the required exception-handling contract.

Add a changed-catch checkpoint to the reviewer skill and cross-cutting guidance. Reviewers must distinguish primary errors from secondary logging, cleanup, callback, or recovery failures, and retain concrete policy uncertainties in `UNRESOLVED`. Deduplication prevents repeat publication but must not silently resolve the underlying concern. Explicit best-effort contracts remain valid counterevidence; an empty catch alone is not a finding. Do not invent a failure producer where the selected source rules it out. Re-read exact old/head paths before reporting an apparent source/diff mismatch.

Static tool-result guards require actual source/guidance reads and reject completed root-wide searches; binary semantic grading checks the producer-to-effect trace and disposition separately. Issues.Body:
## Summary

Prototype for declarative `:debounce` and `:throttle` event modifiers in Blazor.

This PR is the runtime half of a cross-repository work for #10522 (paired with the Razor compiler charge in https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/pull/86312). It enables declarative `@on{EVENT}:debounce="ms"` and `@on{EVENT}:throttle="ms"` directives that rate-limit DOM events on the client before they cross the JS interop or SignalR boundary.

The features can be tried in the sample app under `src/Components/Samples/BlazorWebAppPerPage`.

## Architecture

The end-to-end pipeline follows the same architecture used for `@on{EVENT}:preventDefault` and `@on{EVENT}:stopPropagation`:

1. **Compile-time event metadata (`[EventHandler]`):** Just as `EventHandlerAttribute` declares `enableStopPropagation` and `enablePreventDefault` on `EventHandlers`, a new constructor overload adds `EventThrottleMode` (`Leading` for discrete actions like `onclick` and `onkeydown`, and `LeadingAndTrailing` for continuous state events like `oninput`, `onscroll`, and `onmousemove`).
2. **Render-tree representation (`WebRenderTreeBuilderExtensions`):** Following `AddEventPreventDefaultAttribute` and `AddEventStopPropagationAttribute`, the new `AddEventDebounceAttribute` and `AddEventThrottleAttribute` extension methods emit `__internal_debounce_{event}` and `__internal_throttle_{event}` attribute frames. Representing these modifiers as internal attributes allows them to be added, updated, and removed through existing render-tree diffing with no changes to the `RenderBatch` binary protocol.
3. **Client-side delegation (`BrowserRenderer` & `EventDelegator`):** `BrowserRenderer.applyInternalAttribute` routes `__internal_debounce_*` and `__internal_throttle_*` to `EventDelegator` alongside `preventDefault_*` and `stopPropagation_*`. `EventDelegator` schedules timers per `(element, eventName)`, executes `preventDefault`/`stopPropagation` synchronously on the raw DOM event, protects in-progress user input from stale re-renders in `DomSpecialPropertyUtil`, and flushes pending delayed updates before subsequent commit or action events (`blur`, `change`, `submit`, `click`).

Issues.Title: Remember me isPersistent understanding
Issues.Body:
This is more of a question but its not enough of a question that i could post it up on stack overflow without risking it just getting closed as primary opinion based or to broad.   So i am going to put it here in hopes of getting an answer.

The issue is the understanding of how remember me is supposed to work.    My problem is that its not doing what we would expect it to do.   

Management expects when a user logs in and clicks remember me that they will then not be required to type their login and password again for a month.  Whether or not they will still have to type in the 2fa code is up for debate.

What is actually happening is that i can close the browser reboot and come back for about an hour and 15 minutes and then i will be forced to type my password again.    This still happens even with a valid `.AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie set that is not due to expire for another month.

After digging around in the code i found that Remember me is actually isPersistent and it is defined as.

>Flag indicating whether the sign-in cookie should persist after the browser is closed.

Which brings you to:

There are two different types of Cookies:

- session cookies, held in memory, and which expire once the browser exits
- persistent cookies, which have a time-to-live, are persisted on disk, and are sent by the browser until their time-to-live has elapsed.

All this being said remember machine 2fa works as expected i am not prompted again for the 2fa and i have a cookie on my machine `Identity.TwoFactorRememberMe`.

So I guess my question is why are we not getting a `Identity.FactorRememberMe` or why isn't sign in respecting a long life time of the `AspNetCore.Identity.Application` cookie?

How is this supposed to work exactly?   I am following the code here even though we have normal MVC and not razor pages like you have in the example.  I am still just calling 

>var signInUserResult = await _signInManager.PasswordSignInAsync(userName, password, rememberMe, true);

Note: I am using Asp .net Identity in Identity server 4 application.

Issues.Title: Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?
Issues.Body:
https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/microsoft.aspnetcore.identity.entityframeworkcore.identityuser?view=aspnetcore-1.1

I'm looking through various implementations from the [readme](https://github.com/aspnet/Identity/blob/master/README.md) and I've noticed they all use `IdentityUser ` for their concrete type to pass to `UserManager`, or have had to craft a custom type to be able to have a contract between the database and the .NET AspNetIdentity implentation they've written (see the DynamoDB library).

I've had to do this too for the [Marten implementation I've written](https://github.com/yetanotherchris/Marten.AspNetIdentity), and the reason is, a `TUser` that your `UserStore` takes, should really be an interface - it will always have an email, most likely an Id of some sort, firstname, lastname and then a bag of properties.

Things become even more abstract when dealing with claims.

If everyone is using `IdentityUser` or their own custom `TUser` doesn't this defeat the purpose of AspnetIdentity - which is to be able to switch and change implementations easily? That isn't possible if your consumer is tightly coupled with a `TUser` implementation of the library.

### Example `TUser` implementations

- [MongoIdentityUser](https://github.com/tugberkugurlu/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.MongoDB/MongoIdentityUser.cs)
- [DynamoIdentityUser](https://github.com/miltador/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/blob/master/src/AspNetCore.Identity.DynamoDB/DynamoIdentityUser.cs)
- [Redis uses `IdentityUser<string>`](https://github.com/aguacongas/Identity.Redis/blob/develop/src/Aguacongas.Identity.Redis/UserStore.cs)
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Should IdentityUser be in the EntityFramework namespace?" (#2056)

Issues.Body:
Apologize if my feedback may sound controversial or may spark a debate.

I need to be sure that the problem mentioned on this [page](https://github.com/aspnet/Tooling/blob/master/known-issues-vs2017.md#to-create-aspnet-core-10--11-projects-install-visual-studios-net-core-10---11-developer-tools-for-web-component) about .NET Core 1.0/1.1 tooling is installed when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project should not happen or should not be supported in VS 2019.

These are my main concerns:

1. VS 2019 is about to be released in around early 2019
2. ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 is not going to be supported anymore, based on [this page](https://github.com/dotnet/core/blob/master/microsoft-support.md).
3. Creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 will always install the .NET Core 1.0/1.1 web tooling, and this is not necessary when previous reason has reached the unsupported period and it's quite near or might be the same time of VS 2019 release.
4. Based on the problem mentioned above, VS 2017 has no "built in" tooling when creating new ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 project, but the external tooling may help. Therefore for those that still need to maintain ASP.NET Core 1.0/1.1 projects, we could use VS 2017 as long as the VS 2017 is still in support lifecycle or in mainstream support lifecycle.

I welcome feedback 🙂

Issues.Title: Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json
Issues.Body:
I used to be able to use `dotnet watch` in Visual Studio by adding the following section to `launchSettings.json` and starting the project without debugging using CTRL + F5.

```
    "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    },
```

This used to work in ASP.NET Core 1.1 but no longer does. According to https://github.com/aspnet/DotNetTools/issues/404 the new format for ASP.NET Core 2.0 is:

```
   "Kestrel (dotnet watch run)": {
      "commandName": "Executable",
      "executablePath": "C:\\Program Files\\dotnet\\dotnet.exe",
      "commandLineArgs": "watch run",
      "workingDirectory": "C:\\Users\\namc\\source\\repos\\WebApplication2\\WebApplication2",
      "launchBrowser": true,
      "launchUrl": "https://localhost:5001/",
      "environmentVariables": {
        "ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT": "Development"
      }
    }
```

The problem with this is the hard coded `executablePath` which is Windows specific and the `workingDirectory` which is specific to wherever I did a Git clone on my local machine.
Issues.RelatedDescription: Closed issue "Support dotnet watch in launchSettings.json" (#1067)

Issues.Title: Nesting bug
Issues.Body:
The is a problem nesting embedded resources.  I was experimenting with nesting .cshtml files using the existing rules and did this:

Modal.cs (bootstrap modal web component)
   -> Modal.cs.cshtml (it's view file)

`Modal.cs.cshtml` is set to Embedded Resource, and clearly shows it, but is completed IGNORED by the build process (simply open the DLL in a text editor [such as Notepad++] and scroll to the bottom and look for text).  If I rename the file to "Modal.cshtml" instead it works perfectly fine!  :/  I don't think whether or not a file is embedded should have and role in excluding a file from being embedded so this seems like a bug to me.

Yes, I'm aware of upcoming nesting controls in v15.6, but I'm not able to install it yet, and regardless, this should work fine, so it should be looked into nonetheless.

Just to add: I'm using wild-cards to include the file.  If I explicitly add it I get this:

`Duplicate 'EmbeddedResource' items were included. ...`
